translations.text: "Alas, Eve," said Adam, "you have now badly marked out the fate of the two of us!
Now you can see black hell gaping greedily; now you can hear it raging from here. The kingdom of heaven is not like such flame:

this was the most beautiful of all lands, which we two might have kept here through our Lord's favour, if you had not listened to the one who advised this harm for us, so that we broke the word of the Ruler, the King of Heaven.
Now, sorrowful, we two may grieve over our fate, because he himself commanded us to guard ourselves against such punishment, the greatest of harms.
Now hunger and thirst already torment me, bitter painful affliction, which we were both free of before.
How shall we live now, or how shall we exist in this daylight, now that at times the wind comes here from the west or the east, from the south or the north?
Dark clouds drive up, a cloud of hail comes pressing from the sky, and it moves along together with them (that is terribly cold). At other times the heat shines from the sky, the bright sun blazes:
we two stand here naked like this, unprotected by clothing. There is nothing here in front of us, either for shade or for shelter, and no store of food has been set aside here for us.
We have made mighty God, the Ruler, angry with us. What is to become of us now?
Now I may regret that I ever asked it of God of the heavenly kingdom, the Ruler, th[?]

Then he went off to his dwelling. He had committed a bitter sin against his brother. He left him lying behind his back in a deep valley, weary and bloody, bereft of life, occupying his deathbed, the man on the gravel.
Then God himself spoke to him, the Ruler, with his words (he was angry in his mind, enraged at the slayer), and asked where he had put his brother, the young man.
Then Cain answered him in turn. He had committed a great harmful work with his hands, evil deeds; this world was so badly defiled with sins.
"I need not be concerned with this," he said, "or watch where he goes. God did not command me that I should have to guard anyone here, to watch over him in this world."
"For he firmly believed that he could conceal it from his Lord and hide the deed. Then our Lord spoke to him again: "You have brought it all about in such a way," he said,
"that for the rest of your life your mind may be sorrowful over what you did with your hands, that you became your brother's slayer."
now he lies bloody, weary from wounds. He had done you no wrong and committed no sin against you, yet you have now struck him down and killed him.
His blood now sinks into the earth, his blood lies apart. His soul wanders, his spirit in distress, in God's will;
his blood cries out to the Lord himself and tells who committed the deed, the crime in this middle-world:
no man in the world could do a man worse wrong through bitter evil deeds than the crime you have committed against your brother."
Then Cain grew afraid after the Lord's words, and said that he knew well that none of his deeds could be hidden from the Ruler in this lifetime,
"so now I must carry a troubled mind in my breast," he said, "because I slew my brother with the strength of my hands.
"Now I know that I must live under your hatred, in your enmity from now on, since I have committed these crimes. My sins now seem heavier to me,
my misdeeds greater, than your merciful mind. So I am not worthy, good Ruler, that you should release me from these hateful things and free me from my sorrows.

Since I would not keep my faith and my mind toward your pure heart, I now know that I cannot live here for any length of time. Whoever finds me on these roads will cut me down and slay me for these sins."
Then the Ruler of heaven himself answered him: "You shall still live here," he said, "in this land for a long while.
Though you are hateful in this way, caught up in crimes, I will still give you peace and show you such a sign that you may live in safety in this world, though you are not worthy of it.
Yet from now on you shall live as a fugitive and an outcast in this land, for as long as you look on this light.
Pure people shall curse you. You shall never again come to speak with your Lord and exchange words with him there. The vengeance for your brother stands welling up, bitter, in hell."
Then he went away from there with a grim mind. God himself had utterly rejected him.
Then sorrow was made known there to Adam and Eve, great grief: their child's death, that he could no longer live.
Because of this Adam's mind within his breast was deeply sorrowful when he knew that his son was dead. So too was the mother who had nursed the boy, the child at her breast.
When she washed the bloody grave-clothes, her heart grew sore.
Both of them were then in sorrow, both over their child's death, the young man's departure, and over the fact that Cain had killed him with his hands in such a murder.
At that time they had no other living children in the light except the one, who had then become hateful to the Ruler because of his misdeeds.
They could take no joy in him, because he had raised such hatred that he became his brother's slayer. Because of this both of them, the two spouses, were sore at heart.
Often they stood mourning in tears, the spouses together. They said they knew that their sins had done this to them, that they could not afterward have heirs and sons grow up.
They both suffered great, deadly torment, until mighty God, the lord and guardian of heaven, afterward healed their minds,
so that heirs were granted to them, sons and daughters, who afterward grew up well. They grew beautiful and learned wisdom and wise speech.
The holy Lord furthered the strength of his handiwork, so that a son was born to them. With true words they gave him the name Seth.

The Ruler of heaven gave him growth, a good mind and a cheerful bearing. He was worthy in God's eyes. He was gracious in his heart toward Him, as it goes well for the man who is ever allowed to serve the Lord with such devotion.
He then praised God's favour most among the children of men. From him came good men, wise in words. They learned wisdom, became thoughtful men, and grew up well.
But from Cain, on the other hand, came powerful people, hard-hearted men. They had strong minds and hostile wills. They would not carry out the Ruler's teaching, but kept up hateful strife.
they grew up huge, like giants: that was the worse offspring, descended from Cain. Then the men began to buy wives from one another:
by this Seth's kin was soon corrupted. The people of men became mixed with wickedness, and the children of men became a people hateful to him who created this light,
except that one of them had a nobleman's mind, a thane's way of thinking. He was an excellent man, wise and skilled in speech, and he had great understanding: he was called Enoch.
He became famous among men here on earth, throughout this middle world, because the best of kings [took] him from here still alive, living in his body,
so that he never died in this light. Instead, the ruler of heaven fetched him from here and set him there,
where he may always be in joy, until heaven's guardian sends him back into this world to the children of men, as a teacher for the people.

Then the hateful one will also come here: Antichrist will lead the whole nation, the whole host, astray. Then with a weapon, with sharp edges, by the strength of his hand, he will become Enoch's slayer;
the soul, the spirit, will turn onto the good way. Then God's angel will come and avenge him on the evildoer with the edges of weapons: Antichrist will be robbed of life, the fiend struck down.
The people, the companies of men, will be turned back to God's kingdom for a long while, and afterwards this land will stand safe for them.

Then the people of Sodom, the men, had sinned so badly that our ruler, the mighty Lord, was angry with them, because they practised wickedness and committed crimes. The children of fiends had taught them so much evil:
then the ruling God, the lord, would not put up with it. He commanded three, his angels, to go from the east on his errand and journey to Sodom, and he himself was there with them.

When the mighty ones travelled over Mamre, they found Abraham standing by a temple, keeping watch over a holy place. The best of men was to perform our ruler's sacrifice and to serve God there at midday.
When he saw them coming, he recognized God's power. He went to meet them and bowed down to God himself. He bent low and prayed, and asked earnestly that he might keep his favour from then on:
"Where do you wish to go now, ruler, my lord, almighty father?
I am your own servant, loyal and obedient. You are so good a lord to me, so generous with treasures: Lord, do you wish to have anything of mine? Lo!
It all rests on your judgement. I live by what you have granted me, and I believe in you, my good lord. May I ask you now, Lord of victory, where you wish to journey?"
Then God's answer came back to him, mighty words: "I will not keep it from you now," he said, "or hide from a loyal man where my mind is set.
We are to travel south from here: the men around the land of Sodom have sinned so badly.

Now the guardians cry out to me day and night. They recount their deeds and tell of their sins. Now I want to find out for myself whether those men commit such wickedness among themselves, such evil deeds.

If so, raging fire shall fall upon them, and their grievous crimes and sins shall sink them. Sulphur will fall from heaven with fire, and the wicked will die, the men of evil deeds, just as morning comes."
Then Abraham spoke (he had good courage and wise words), and spoke to his Ruler: "Lo! You decree so much good," he said,
"God, Ruler of the heavenly kingdom, Lord; this whole world stands by your deeds, according to your will.

you have power over this middle-earth, over the race of men, so that it shall never happen, my lord and ruler, that you treat evil and good there as one, the loved and the hated, for they are not alike.
You glory in such justice, mighty Lord, that you do not wish good-willed men there to pay for the work of wicked evildoers, though you have the power to do it.
May I ask you now, if you will not be angry with me for it, God of the kingdom of heaven?
If you find there fifty righteous men, living people, may that land then stand safe, ruler, protected by your will?"
Then God's answer came back to him: "If I find fifty there," he said,
"pious men, good men, who have held fast to God, then I will spare their lives, because I want to preserve those pure men."
Abraham then spoke a second time and questioned his Lord further: "What will you do then," he said,
"my Lord and master, if you can find thirty thanes there, men without stain? Will you still let them live, so that they may keep the land?"
Then the good one, God of the heavenly kingdom, quickly told him that he would do so in that land: "If I can find there," he said,
"thirty faithful thanes among that people, God-fearing men, then I will forgive them all the crime and the misdeeds, and let that people live around Sodom and be safe."
Then Abraham spoke earnestly, pressing his Lord, and said many words: "Now I must ask you this," he said,
"that you not be angry with me, my good Lord, because I speak so much and trade words with you like this:
I know that I am not worthy of it, unless you, God of the kingdom of heaven, Lord, are willing to bear with it out of your goodness;
I have great need to know your will: whether the people who are to lie dead, fallen as doomed men, may live on in safety.
What will you do then, my lord, if you can find ten faithful, righteous men there among the people?
Will you then grant them their life, so that they may live around the land of Sodom and dwell in the towns, and you are not angry with them?"
Then God's answer came back to him: "If I can still find ten faithful people there in the land," he said, "then I will let them all keep their life for the sake of the righteous men."

Then Abraham did not dare to question his lord any longer. Instead, the strong man fell on his knees in prayer after him. He said that he would gladly prepare [?] his offering and serve God, and do his will.
Then he went back from there to his dwelling. God's angels travelled on to Sodom, as the Ruler himself had commanded with his word when he told them to go on their way.
They were to find out how many righteous men there were around the city of Sodom, men free of sins, who had not done much crime or wickedness.
Then they heard the clamour of the doomed [?] in every dwelling, sinful people committing wicked deeds:
There was a throng of fiends there, hostile creatures, who had led the people astray into that wickedness. The reward was then at hand, great and deadly, for their having so often committed crimes.

There sat within the city a man of noble birth, Lot, among the people, who often worked the praise of God in this world. He had there plenty of wealth, goods he had gained. He was worthy in God's sight.
He was of Abraham's noble kin, his brother's child. There was no better man, with manly virtues, around the shores of the Jordan; he was endowed with wisdom. Our Ruler was gracious to him.
When the white sun sank to its seat, the brightest of all beacons, he stood before the city's gate.
Then in the evening he saw two angels walking into the dwellings, as they came from God, endowed with wisdom. At once he spoke to them with his words.
He went toward them and thanked God, heaven's king, for granting him the help that he might look upon them with his eyes,
and he kissed them on the knee and courteously asked them to visit his dwelling. He said that he would give them their own choice of whatever goods God had granted him in the land.
They were not at all too slow, but went into his guest-hall, and he served them devoutly. They told him many true words.
There he sat in watch, and kept his Lord's messengers, God's angels, in holiness. They told him so much that was good and true.
The dark, narrow night glided on into the clouds; morning drew near to every dwelling. The dawn-bird sang before the day's glory.
Then our Lord's messengers had found out the crimes that men committed around the city of Sodom.
Then they told Lot that a great slaughter of the children of men must come upon the people there, and likewise upon the land.
They told him to make ready and to go away from there, to remove himself from the fiends and to lead his wife with him, the nobly born woman.
He had no more of his kin there except his two daughters. With them, they commanded, he was to be up on a mountain before day, so that the burning fire would not catch him.

When he had hastily made ready for the journey, the angels, the messengers of heaven's king, set off. They held him by the hands, led him and instructed him for a long while, until they had brought him out beyond the city.
They commanded that, however great a crash they heard, a breaking in the cities, they must never look behind them, if they wished to live in the land.
Then the holy guardians, God's angels, turned back again, went swiftly, and journeyed to Sodom.
From there Lot travelled southward, following their instruction, and fled the throng of the people, of wicked men. Then day had come.

Then a great crash arose there, reaching to heaven; it burst and cracked. Every one of the cities was filled with smoke, so much fire had fallen there from the sky. There was an outcry of the doomed, of the hateful people.

Flame seized all the broad city-settlements. Everything burned together, stone and earth, and so many hostile men died and sank. Burning sulphur surged through the dwellings; the outlaws suffered a hateful reward.
The land sank in, the earth into the abyss. All the realm of Sodom was destroyed, so that not a single man survived, and it was deadened into a Dead Sea, as it still stands today, filled with water.
Then all the people of Sodom had paid dearly for their crimes, except that the Ruler, by his will, had led one of them out of there, and the women with him: three with the thane.

Then they heard the death-agony of the people, the cities burning. Then a nobly born woman looked back behind her: she would not carry out the teaching of the angels (that was Lot's wife), for as long as she was allowed to live in that land.
When she stood on the hill and looked back behind her, she was turned to stone. There she shall stand as a famous sign to men across middle-earth, from now on forever, as long as this earth lives.
